items.originalTitle: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
items.author: Adam Wren
items.title: Buttigieg allies launch effort to back another presidential run
items.summary: Allies of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg are launching an independent, grassroots effort urging him to undertake a second presidential campaign ahead of 2028. Team Pete PAC will be led by Jennifer Holdsworth, the former national campaign manager of Buttigieg’s unsuccessful 2017 bid for DNC chair, and Mohsin Syed, his former chief of staff at the Transportation Department. The PAC is aiming to bring together volunteers and grassroots donors who backed Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential bid. “Mohsin and I have traveled the country this year, and everywhere we go, people ask us the same question: how can I help Pete?” Holdsworth said in a statement. Team Pete PAC is independent and has no ties to Buttigieg’s Win the Era PAC, nor is it a presidential committee. Through Win the Era, Buttigieg campaigned with 102 candidates across the map for the midterms, visiting 38 states (19 of them twice). Asked on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday whether he had a timeline to make a decision, Buttigieg said he would be “surprised” if he was the first potential 2028 presidential candidate “to make news” and said he’s “certainly not cooking up anything to announce in the next few weeks.” Even as it forms to press Buttigieg to mount a second presidential campaign, Team Pete PAC is urging potential backers to take part in community service — a nod to Buttigeig’s proposed national service program he proposed as a candidate. “I’ve seen up close what Pete can do,” Syed said. “He has a unique ability to bring people together and inspire action.”

items.originalTitle: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
items.author: Lauren Fedor
items.title: Oklahoma GOP governor warns of growing socialist tendencies on the right
items.summary: Oklahoma’s Republican governor warned against populist economic ideas gaining popularity, as he called for fellow Republicans to reject socialism and embrace free markets and an “ownership economy.” “A socialist or a populist economy is something that is not American,” Gov. Kevin Stitt said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. “We should all be concerned about the amount of people that think that socialism is the answer.” When asked if he was concerned about socialist tendencies on the right, Stitt criticized fellow Republicans who have called for data center moratoriums.. “When you start dictating … you see some people from the far right saying, ‘Well, we don’t want data centers. We don’t want that,’” Stitt said. “When did we become a party that if you follow all the rules, you follow the permitting, the clean water, the clean air, and you own your own land, that we allow the government to tell you what you can do on that property?” the Oklahoma governor asked. “That is what I'm talking about, that we need to be very, very careful about.” Stitt also called on President Donald Trump to use his final two years in the White House to push for bipartisan immigration reform — his latest remarks on the topic. “We need to have a strong border. We need to know who is coming into our country. We need to vet those people,” Stitt told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “He can lead on this, he can fix this immigration policy. “To me, we are overthinking it,” Stitt added. “It is as simple as: If an employer is vouching for an employee, the state governors should be able to issue that workforce permit. Period, end of story.” Stitt described Trump as a “business person” who “understands the need for a workforce.” But he blamed Congress and other interests in Washington for standing in the way of reform. “It's not that complicated. But the problem is Washington, D.C., each side thinks they're winning on it. They raise money off of it. They politic off of it. They try to crush the other side over these issues instead of fixing it for the American people,” Stitt said. “That's why you saw this huge swing in the midterms.”

items.originalTitle: 2026’s Words of the Year, So Far
items.author: Chad de Guzman
items.title: 2026’s Words of the Year, So Far
items.summary: —Malte Mueller—Getty Images It can be difficult to sum up a year in a word, but that hasn’t stopped dictionaries from trying. Last year , they picked terms like “rage bait,” “AI slop,” and even the slang 67 (pronounced six-seven), in attempts to capture the cultural zeitgeist. For 2026, some dictionaries have already begun to announce their “word of the year.” Read More: Words of the Year: How the Pithy Tradition Began Each dictionary approaches the selection differently—some track language use or online search trends—and some even offer shortlists of what other words were considered. Here are some of 2026’s words of the year, so far. Cambridge Dictionary: human Cambridge Dictionary, which has picked a word of the year since 2015, announced it chose “human” for 2026 in response to the prevalence of AI and breakthroughs in the technology. “The year was defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines,” the dictionary’s announcement said. Cambridge noted in a blog post that the word had increasingly appeared in compounds like “human-written” and “human-generated.” In its announcement, Cambridge also cited public figures, such as Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton or Pope Leo XIV , who have used the word when speaking about AI and what humanity can do in turn. It referred to Pope Leo XIV ’s statements about remaining “profoundly human” at the age of AI , and artists’ rejection of the “ assault on human creativity” in recent years. “AI is changing how we talk about being human,” Cambridge’s lexicographer Colin McIntosh said. “Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children.” Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, said that he thinks the choice is “interesting” because “right now our understanding of humanity is changing.” “Human” was chosen among other contenders—some of which were also related to rapid technology development, such as “ agent ” (referring to an AI system that autonomously functions on behalf of humans) and “ analogue ” (in opposition to digital-centric lifestyles). Collins Dictionary: mogging Collins Dictionary, which began selecting its word of the year in 2013, delved into Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang for its 2026 pick: “ mogging ,” which it defines as “the act of outshining or outperforming someone or something.” Collins said the word is believed to have come from the slang noun “mog,” which meant a dominant male and is, in turn, a shortening of AMOG, an acronym for “Alpha Male Of the Group.” According to Collins, the word has been used since around 2016, emerging in bodybuilding culture to refer to the gym’s most physically dominant male. But it gained new life in the “ manosphere ,” the mostly-online cultural network revolving around masculinity, men’s issues, and, often, anti-feminism. It’s been increasingly used by famous figures, too. In June, the White House’s official X account used a form of the word. “Mogged,” read a caption for a photo of President Donald Trump holding a poster board that compared the length of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the height of popular skyscrapers. U.S. figure skater Alysa Liu , who won gold in the 2026 Winter Olympics , had said that her main goal was “ to mog .” Former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger also shared on social media that someone had explained “frame-mogging” to him, along with a montage of clips flexing his physique in his bodybuilding days. https://x.com/WhiteHouse/status/2062318641542988097 Collins’ shortlist of other contenders for the word of the year were carspreading , which it defined as “the tendency of car manufacturers to build vehicles that are longer, wider and heavier,” and firewave , a British English climate change -related compound that means “a series of urban wildfires within a short period of time, usually caused by an extended period of hot, dry weather,” which Europe experienced this summer. Dictionary.com: maxxing Dictionary.com, which has announced a word of the year since 2010, picked for 2026 the Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang term “maxxing,” which it said could both stand on its own and be affixed to another word—to indicate that an object, aspect, or activity is being optimized. “Maxxing” beat others on Dictionary.com’s shortlist, which included “ affordability ,” “ data center ,” “ odyssey ,” and “ unc .” With roots in words like “maximum” and “maximize,” the word “maxxing,” according to Dictionary.com, branched out from the gaming term “min-maxing,” which meant strategizing to shape a game character’s strengths to make weaknesses relatively negligible. Dictionary.com theorizes that somewhere along the way, the “min-” part got dropped, and it found an extra “x.” “Maxxing” went mainstream in the suffix form of “looksmaxxing.” In 2023, the New York Times reported on so-called “ looksmaxxers ,” a digital community of mostly young men who are trying to “mog,” in the belief that achieving peak physical masculinity would guarantee them success in their romantic lives. While some resorted to controlled diets and rigorous exercise regimens, others took “looksmaxxing” to extremes , such as repeated cosmetic surgeries and chemical modifications and even “bonesmashing.” Dictionary.com said in its announcement that searches for “maxxing” and related terms spiked in 2026, and that “maxxing” has also taken hold beyond the manosphere. In health, some people have turned to practices like fibermaxxing , proteinmaxxing , and sleepmaxxing . The word has also been used to describe cultural phenomena: earlier this year, a growing fascination with China and Chinese culture led social media users to embrace “ Chinamaxxing .” The word “captures the very 2026 urge to keep pushing harder while also giving us a way to poke fun at ourselves when optimizing our lives starts to feel absurd,” the online dictionary said. “The open question is whether this need for optimization has peaked or if we’ll push even harder next year. Maxxingmaxxing, anyone?”
